A B-tree index organizes sorted keys in a balanced multiway tree that supports efficient equality lookups and range scans. Each node contains multiple keys and child pointers, so the tree has a high branching factor and remains shallow even for large data sets.

The root is the starting point. Internal nodes function as decision points: they compare the search key against their stored keys and direct the query to the appropriate subtree. Leaf nodes, all located at the same level, store the actual index entries—typically the indexed values together with row locators that point into the table.

Insertions and deletions may cause node splits or merges to keep the tree balanced and to maintain a minimum number of keys per node. Because every root-to-leaf path has approximately the same length, access time is logarithmic and predictable. Nodes are sized to match disk pages, minimizing I/O. Once the starting leaf for a range is found, subsequent leaves can be read sequentially thanks to the sorted order.
